summary: Describes using keyed SHA-1 with the IP Authentication Header. The document is historic.

eli5.summary: A secret-key stamp lets you prove a packet came from the right sender and was not changed. This described one such stamp for IP packets, and it is now only of historic interest.

questions: keyed sha1 with ip authentication header
how does keyed sha1 work with ip authentication header
subtitle: A historic recipe for authenticating IP packets by hashing them with a secret key on both sides, using SHA1.

tldr.problem: The IP Authentication Header needs a keyed algorithm that proves an IP datagram came from the holder of a shared secret and was not changed.
tldr.mechanism: SHA1-IP-MAC hashes the padded secret key, the invariant parts of the datagram, and the key again. The 160-bit digest, or a 128-bit truncation, goes in the Authentication Data field.
tldr.outcome: This document is Historic. It replaced RFC 1852 and is kept only as a record of the method.

today: RFC 2841 is Historic. It obsoletes RFC 1852 and is not an Internet standard, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: What IP-MAC Does
sections.content:
The Authentication Header (AH, RFC 1826) provides integrity and authentication for IP datagrams. This specification defines how AH uses keys with the Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA1). The SHA1-IP-MAC algorithm uses a leading and trailing key, a variant of the envelope method, with alignment padding between the keys and the data.

The document specifies the corrected SHA described in FIPS-180-1, which is not interoperable with the older, flawed version. It assumes the reader knows the Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol (RFC 1825).
sections.eli5: This describes one way to stamp each internet packet with a secret-based fingerprint so a receiver can trust it.

sections.title: Keys
sections.content: The secret authentication key shared by the two parties SHOULD be a cryptographically strong random number, not a guessable string. The transform does not limit key size. Implementations MUST support 160-bit (20 octet) keys, though a particular key may be shorter, and longer keys are encouraged.
sections.eli5: The shared secret should be hard to guess, like a long random password, not your pet's name.

sections.title: Output Size and Alignment
sections.content:
SHA1 produces 160 bits, which is naturally 32-bit aligned, but many implementations want the following headers 64-bit aligned. Four options are listed, most preferred first:

  1. Use only the most significant 128 bits (16 octets) of output.
  2. Add 32 bits (4 octets) of padding before the SHA1 output.
  3. Add 32 bits (4 octets) of padding after the output.
  4. Place the output at a variable bit position within 192 bits (24 octets).

The size and position are negotiated as part of key management. Padding bits hold unspecified, implementation-dependent values that are ignored on receipt. The RFC adds that truncation may even improve robustness, according to some analysts.
sections.eli5: The fingerprint has to fit neatly in a box. You can trim it or add blank filler so it lines up.

sections.title: The Calculation
sections.content:
The authenticated message has the form SHA1( key, keyfill, datagram, datafill, key, sha1fill ). The steps are:

  1. Fill the variable-length key to the next 512-bit boundary with the pad-with-length technique defined for SHA1, which includes the length.
  2. Append the invariant fields of the whole IP datagram, with variant fields zeroed, and fill to the next 512-bit boundary. The length covers the leading key and the data.
  3. Append the original key again; SHA1 adds its own trailing pad-with-length.
  4. Compute the 160-bit digest and insert it in the Authentication Data field.

The leading key is padded so it can be copied at machine boundaries without realigning the datagram, and so it can be prehashed. The trailing key is not needed against appending attacks, because the IP datagram has a total length field, but it mixes the whole key in again and protects very long and very short datagrams. Implementations that add keys and padding in place must not let the link driver send them.
sections.eli5: Put your secret on both ends of the message, fill gaps with filler, scramble it all, and keep the scrambled result as the fingerprint.

sections.title: Performance
sections.content: Preliminary results said SHA1 is 62% as fast as MD5 and 80% as fast as DES hashing. The RFC judged this a reasonable trade, since SHA1's internal chaining is significantly longer than DES or MD5. It asks for suggestions of faster, patent-free alternatives with adequate cryptographic strength.
sections.eli5: It is a bit slower than some older scramblers, but the scramble is harder to break.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security provided depends completely on the strength of SHA1, the correctness of its implementation, the key management mechanism, the strength of the key, and correct implementations in all participating nodes. SHA was derived from MD4 (RFC 1320), and a flaw was apparently found in the original specification, which this document corrects.

At the time of writing there were no known attacks on SHA1 better than brute force, and its 160-bit hash is far more resistant to brute force than the 128-bit MD4 and MD5. The RFC warns that cryptographers are fallible and deficiencies may yet be found.
sections.eli5: The lock is only as strong as the scrambler, the secret and the people using it. The authors said no one had broken it yet, but might later.
